Winston Churchill. On May 13, 1940, just three days after becoming Prime Minister, he addressed Parliament at the darkest moment of British history. Nazi Germany had invaded France, and the prospects for Britain seemed bleak. Yet Churchill offered no false hope.

"I have nothing to offer but blood, toil, tears and sweat," he declared. He set the war's singular purpose: victory at all costs, victory in spite of all terror, victory however long and hard the road may be. He spoke of the abyss of a new Dark Age if Britain failed, grounding the struggle in existential terms. Behind them, he acknowledged, stood a group of shattered states and bludgeoned races.

The speech explicitly rejected the appeasement policy of the previous government, signaling a complete strategic reversal. Churchill established himself as the voice of grim, unflinching resolve—a tone he maintained throughout the war. His words offered no comfort, only an unbreakable will to resist. That tone of steely determination made him the embodiment of British resistance and shaped the nation's defiance for the years of warfare ahead.
